title: The Geometry of a Round Sukkah
subtitle: Working out exactly why Rabbi Yochanan's 24-amos circumference is bigger than the math strictly requires — and whether that's a problem.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 1-3 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 8. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).
before: 7b ended with a math problem: Rabbi Yochanan requires a round sukkah to seat 24 people, but a quick calculation suggested 12 should be enough to match Rabbi's 4×4-amos square minimum. This amud is that calculation, done properly and re-checked twice.

It's real geometry — inscribed circles and squares, the ratio between a square's side and its diagonal — used entirely in service of one halachic number. Watch for the Gemara correcting its own math twice before landing on an answer it's satisfied with.

flow.label: First correction: a circle inscribed in a square isn't the same as a square inscribed in a circle
flow.sub: the two ratios go in different directions — Rabbi Yochanan's case is the harder one

flow.label: Precise calculation: a circumference of 16⅘ amos should suffice
flow.sub: using the rule that a square's diagonal is about 1.4× its side

flow.label: So why does Rabbi Yochanan require 24?

items.label: First attempt: he wasn't being precise
items.sub: rejected — the gap (24 vs. 16.8) is too large to wave away as imprecision

items.label: Second attempt: he's counting 3 people per 2 amos, not 1 per amos
items.sub: gets to 16.8 amos almost exactly — but still doesn't explain 24

items.label: Third attempt: he's measuring the inner circle formed by the seated people, not the sukkah's own wall
items.sub: gets to 18 amos — closer, and this time the imprecision runs toward stringency, which is acceptable

flow.label: A completely different calculation offered
flow.sub: the Sages of Caesarea propose measuring by area instead of length — but the Gemara notes real-world measurement doesn't actually bear this out, continuing onto 8b

flowCaption: A halachic number gets a real geometric derivation, corrected twice before landing.

opinions.claim: A round, furnace-shaped sukkah needs a circumference large enough to seat 24 people.
opinions.basis: Matches Rabbi's 4×4-amos square minimum, converted to a circle — via a calculation the Gemara has to reconstruct and correct.

opinions.who: Mar Keshisha, son of Rav Chisda
opinions.claim: People don't each take a full amah when seated — three people fit in two amos.
opinions.basis: A more realistic seating-density assumption, bringing the required circumference down to 16⅘ amos — very close to the precise geometric minimum.

opinions.claim: Rabbi Yochanan's 24-amos figure measures the inner circle formed by the seated people themselves, not the sukkah's own outer wall.
opinions.basis: Produces 18 amos as the precise requirement — closer to 24 than any prior attempt, and importantly errs toward stringency rather than leniency.

script.speaker: First correction
script.quote: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּעִיגּוּלָא, אֲבָל בְּרִיבּוּעָא — בָּעֲיָא טְפֵי.
script.gloss: The earlier 12-amos estimate only works for a circle inscribed inside a square. Rabbi's case needs the reverse — a square (4×4 amos) inscribed inside a circle — which requires a larger circumference.

script.speaker: Gemara quantifies
script.quote: מִכְּדֵי כַּמָּה מְרוּבָּע יוֹתֵר עַל הָעִיגּוּל — רְבִיעַ, בְּשִׁיתְּסַר סַגִּי?
script.gloss: A square's perimeter exceeds an inscribed circle's circumference by a quarter — so 16 amos should be enough. Still not 24.

script.speaker: Second correction
script.quote: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּעִיגּוּל דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ רִיבּוּעָא, אֲבָל רִיבּוּעָא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ עִגּוּלָא — בָּעֵינַן טְפֵי, מִשּׁוּם מוּרְשָׁא דְקַרְנָתָא.
script.gloss: That ratio runs the other direction too. For a square circumscribed by a circle (our actual case), the circle needs to be bigger still, to clear the square's protruding corners.

script.speaker: Gemara does the precise math
script.quote: כׇּל אַמְּתָא בְּרִיבּוּעָא אַמְּתָא וּתְרֵי חוּמְשֵׁי בַּאֲלַכְסוֹנָא, בְּשִׁיבְסַר נְכֵי חוּמְשָׁא סַגִּיא?
script.gloss: Using the rule that a square's diagonal is about 1⅖ times its side (so a 4-amos square has a diagonal, and thus a circumscribing circle's diameter, of about 5⅗ amos), the precise minimum circumference comes out to 17 amos minus a fifth — not 24.

script.speaker: First explanation offered
script.gloss: Rabbi Yochanan simply wasn't being precise — he rounded up.

script.speaker: Gemara rejects it
script.quote: אֵימוֹר דְּאָמְרִינַן לָא דָּק פּוּרְתָּא, טוּבָא מִי אָמְרִינַן לָא דָּק?
script.gloss: "Not being precise" can excuse a small gap — not a difference of more than 7 amos.

script.speaker: Mar Keshisha's correction
script.quote: מִי סָבְרַתְּ גַּבְרָא בְּאַמְּתָא יָתֵיב, תְּלָתָא גַּבְרֵי בְּתַרְתֵּי אַמְּתָא יָתְבִי.
script.gloss: You're assuming each person needs a full amah of seating space — really, three people fit in two amos. On that basis, 24 people need 16 amos of circumference, very close to the precise 16⅘ figure.

script.speaker: Gemara pushes again
script.quote: אֵימוֹר דְּאָמְרִינַן לָא דָּק לְחוּמְרָא, לְקוּלָּא מִי אָמְרִינַן לָא דָּק?
script.gloss: "Not precise" is more tolerable when it makes the law stricter than necessary. But this correction would make Rabbi Yochanan's number a touch lenient relative to the precise minimum — and we don't excuse imprecision that direction.

script.speaker: Rav Asi's reframing
script.quote: לְעוֹלָם גַּבְרָא בְּאַמְּתָא יָתֵיב, וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מְקוֹם גַּבְרֵי לָא קָחָשֵׁיב.
script.gloss: Actually, each person does take a full amah — but Rabbi Yochanan's 24 amos measures only the inner circle traced by the seated people themselves, not the sukkah's actual outer wall circumference.

script.speaker: Checked and accepted
script.quote: כַּמָּה הָווּ לְהוּ — תַּמְנֵי סְרֵי, בְּשִׁיבְסַר נְכֵי חוּמְשָׁא סַגִּיא! הַיְינוּ דְּלָא דָּק וּלְחוּמְרָא לָא דָּק.
script.gloss: That inner circle works out to 18 amos — compared to the precise 17-minus-a-fifth minimum, this is imprecision toward the stringent side, which is acceptable. This explanation stands.

script.speaker: A different approach altogether, continuing to 8b
script.quote: רַבָּנַן דְּקֵיסָרִי... עִיגּוּלָא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ רִיבּוּעָא — רִבְעָא.
script.gloss: The Sages of Caesarea propose a different framework entirely, based on area rather than length — continued on 8b.

tosfos.summary: A geometric proof (condensed here) that the "square is a quarter bigger than an inscribed circle" rule is about area, not the length of a string wrapped around the shape.

points.label: (a)-(b) Why circumference alone doesn't prove it
points.he: אין להוכיח דבר זה מהא דטבלא מרובעת... דאין מביאין ראיה מחוט ההיקף
points.en: You might think a 3×3 square (perimeter 12) versus a circle of diameter 3 (circumference ~9) proves the ratio — but that's the wrong comparison. Splitting a 4×4 square into unit squares gives 16, while a circle of the same diameter holds only about 12 — the same quarter-ratio, but derived from area, not the perimeter/circumference numbers themselves.

points.label: (c) A cleaner geometric proof
points.he: אם באנו לכוין החשבון... שתעשה נקודה של משהו ותקיפנה בחוטין הרבה
points.en: Tosfos constructs the ratio directly: build up a circular Tefach out of concentric threads, cut and unfold them into a triangle, and the resulting area comes out to exactly three-quarters of an equivalent square — confirming the quarter-difference geometrically.

tosfos.summary: Proving that a square's diagonal is actually a bit more than exactly 1⅖ times its side — the Gemara's figure is a rounded approximation.

points.label: Proof by area
points.he: אם תעשה ריבוע של עשר על עשר ותחלק אותו שתי וערב... נמצא דאין בו חציו של חיצון
points.en: A 10×10 square split into diagonal-based quarters gives an inner diamond of exactly 50 square units (half the outer square). But if the diagonal were exactly 1⅖ times the side (giving a 7×7 inner square), that inner square would only measure 49 — not quite half. So the true ratio must be very slightly more than 1⅖.

tosfos.summary: The Gemara's own resolution (Rav Asi's) doesn't actually match how Rabbi Yochanan's measure is used elsewhere.

points.label: (a) Observation
points.he: על חנם דחק ליישב דברי ר' יוחנן דעל כרחך מקום גברי קחשיב
points.en: The Gemara's effort here seems unnecessary — Rabbi Yochanan's own parallel ruling in Eruvin (76a), about a round window needing a 24-tefachim circumference, only makes sense if he does count the people's own space, the very possibility just rejected. The explanation that actually fits there is the Caesarean judges' area-based approach instead.
